strengths: The problem is relevant and well motivated. The analytical example clearly demonstrates how unconditional interventions or an unsuitable fixed policy scope can prevent recovery of the optimal contextual policy.

The averaged-UCB scope-selection index is a concrete algorithmic contribution. Separating scope-selection regret from within-scope optimisation regret provides a useful framework for analysing the approach.

The experiments use 110 random seeds, uncertainty estimates, and a shared BO backend for the main comparisons. Context, noise, and backend ablations provide useful evidence, while the larger synthetic example demonstrates benefits from removing irrelevant dimensions.
weaknesses: The reduction from general mixed policies to the analysed bandit model is not justified. Definition 1 permits a context variable downstream of one intervention and upstream of another, whereas Algorithm 2 observes all contexts before choosing all actions and assumes a fixed context distribution independent of those actions. Moreover, grouping scopes solely by their unions of action and context variables discards the per-action information restrictions. Additional structural restrictions or a proof preserving policy feasibility and optimality are needed.

The central regret proof contains substantive gaps. On page 27, the action loss f_i^*(c) - f_i(x,c) is bounded by the range of f_i^* across contexts. This is false: a function that varies with actions but is constant across contexts can have positive action loss and zero contextual range. The resulting martingale argument therefore requires correction. Additionally, Equation (21) and the concluding derivation use c(T), defined using worst-arm information gain gamma(T), while the stated instance-dependent theorem substitutes the smaller averaged information gain without establishing that improvement.

The theoretical coverage is narrower than the practical claims. The analysis assumes independent GP draws with known kernels, Gaussian homoscedastic noise, compact domains, and exact UCB maximisation. The HEBO implementation learns transformations and surrogate parameters, and several experimental SCMs generate non-Gaussian or action-dependent residual noise. The manuscript does not establish that its guarantees extend to these implementations and environments.

The evaluation does not sufficiently isolate the new algorithmic contribution. Comparisons primarily involve CaBO and CoBO, whose policy restrictions explain several failures by construction. The closest contextual-causal approaches discussed in related work, particularly Functional Causal BO, are not experimentally compared. A comparison using the same POMPS set with alternative scope selectors is also missing; the existing context and backend ablations do not establish the benefit of the averaged-UCB selector.

Scalability claims exceed the evidence. Section 3 explicitly retains brute-force POMPS enumeration with exponential complexity. No enumeration runtime, memory measurements, or scaling study over the number of candidate scopes is provided. The reported environments contain only one or two POMPSs, and the large example mainly adds redundant variables, so it does not establish scalability of scope search.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing implementation details and inconsistent specifications. Although a public implementation is claimed, the manuscript supplies no repository URL or concrete experimental beta/rho settings. In Appendix A.1.2, the stated PSA equation omits Cancer, so the subsequent substitution does not produce the claimed sum of squares or zero optimum. Appendix A.3 defines C4 using itself, contradicting the DAG. Algorithm 2 also falls through from initialisation into selection over incompletely initialised arms. These discrepancies require correction and verification against the experiments.
